title: Αλιεῖς ⟨λίθον ἀγρεύσαντες⟩
titleEn: The Fishermen Who Caught a Stone
part: The Fishermen Who Caught a Stone (Chambry 23 · Perry 13)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 23 (= Perry 13). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἁλιεῖς σαγήνην εἷλκον· βαρείας δὲ αὐτῆς οὔσης, ἔχαιρον καὶ ὠρχοῦντο, πολλὴν εἶναι νομίζοντες τὴν ἄγραν.
sentences.tr: Halieis sagēnēn heilkon· bareias de autēs ousēs, echairon kai ōrchounto, pollēn einai nomizontes tēn agran.
sentences.l: Fishermen were hauling a dragnet; and it being heavy, they rejoiced and danced, thinking the catch to be a great one.
sentences.n: σαγήνη is the big seine, a net worked from the shore by a whole team — hence a crowd of fishermen and a haul heavy enough to dance about. βαρείας δὲ αὐτῆς οὔσης is a genitive absolute, causal here: “since it was heavy.” νομίζω takes accusative and infinitive for what one supposes.

sentences.t: Ὡς δὲ ἀφελκύσαντες ἐπὶ τὴν ἠιόνα τῶν μὲν ἰχθύων ὀλίγους εὗρον, λίθων δὲ καὶ ἄλλης ὕλης μεστὴν τὴν σαγήνην, οὐ μετρίως ἐβαρυθύμουν, οὐ τοσοῦτον ἐπὶ τῷ συμβεβηκότι δυσφοροῦντες ὅσον ὅτι καὶ τὰ ἐναντία προειλήφεισαν.
sentences.tr: Hōs de aphelkysantes epi tēn ēiona tōn men ichthyōn oligous heuron, lithōn de kai allēs hylēs mestēn tēn sagēnēn, ou metriōs ebarythymoun, ou tosouton epi tōi symbebēkoti dysphorountes hoson hoti kai ta enantia proeilēpheisan.
sentences.l: But when, having dragged it up onto the beach, they found few of the fish, but the net full of stones and other matter, they were beyond measure heavy-hearted, not so much distressed at what had happened as because they had also assumed the opposite beforehand.
sentences.i: But when they had dragged it up onto the beach and found few fish in it, and the net full of stones and other rubbish, their spirits sank beyond measure — grieved not so much at what had happened as at having expected the very opposite.
sentences.n: οὐ τοσοῦτον … ὅσον, “not so much … as,” with the second limb changing construction in mid-comparison, from a preposition and noun (ἐπὶ τῷ συμβεβηκότι) to a ὅτι-clause: Greek switches like this more readily than English. τῷ συμβεβηκότι is a perfect participle used as a noun, “the thing that had happened.” προειλήφεισαν is a pluperfect of προλαμβάνω, “they had assumed it in advance.” ὕλη is raw stuff of any kind — timber, matter, here the weed and debris in the net.

sentences.t: Εἷς δέ τις ἐν αὐτοῖς γηραιὸς ὢν εἶπεν· « Ἀλλὰ παυσόμεθα, ὦ ἑταῖροι· χαρᾶς γάρ, ὡς ἔοικεν, ἀδελφή ἐστιν ἡ λύπη, καὶ ἡμᾶς ἔδει τοσαῦτα προησθέντας πάντως παθεῖν τι καὶ λυπηρόν. »
sentences.tr: Heis de tis en autois gēraios ōn eipen· « Alla pausometha, ō hetairoi· charas gar, hōs eoiken, adelphē estin hē lypē, kai hēmas edei tosauta proēsthentas pantōs pathein ti kai lypēron. »
sentences.l: But one among them, being aged, said: « Well, we shall leave off, comrades; for grief, it seems, is joy's sister, and it was necessary that we, having taken so much pleasure beforehand, should altogether suffer something painful too. »
sentences.i: But one of them, an old man, said: « Come, let us leave off, friends; grief, it seems, is joy's sister, and having had so much pleasure beforehand, we were bound to suffer something painful too. »
sentences.n: παυσόμεθα is a future indicative, “we shall stop”; after ἀλλά and a vocative it reads as an exhortation, “let us stop,” though the plain future sense is possible too. ἔδει, the imperfect of δεῖ, with the aorist infinitive παθεῖν, states what had to happen as seen from after the event. προησθέντας is the aorist participle of προήδομαι, “to take pleasure beforehand” — a rare compound, and the whole point of the old man's remark. χαρᾶς … ἀδελφή is a plain genitive of relationship, “sister of joy.”

sentences.t: Ἀτὰρ οὖν καὶ ἡμᾶς δεῖ τοῦ βίου τὸ εὐμετάβλητον ὁρῶντας μὴ τοῖς αὐτοῖς πράγμασιν ἀεὶ ἐπαγάλλεσθαι, λογιζομένους ὅτι ἐκ πολλῆς εὐδίας ἀνάγκη καὶ χειμῶνα γενέσθαι.
sentences.tr: Atar oun kai hēmas dei tou biou to eumetablēton horōntas mē tois autois pragmasin aei epagallesthai, logizomenous hoti ek pollēs eudias anankē kai cheimōna genesthai.
sentences.l: So then we too must, seeing the changeableness of life, not always exult in the same circumstances, reckoning that out of much fair weather a storm too must come.
sentences.i: So we too, seeing how changeable life is, should not always take delight in the same state of things, reckoning that after a long spell of fair weather a storm must come as well.
sentences.n: Ἀτὰρ οὖν καὶ ἡμᾶς, “so then we too” — a closing formula in which the fable turns and takes the reader in; it closes fable 245 the same way. τὸ εὐμετάβλητον is an adjective made a noun by the article, “the easily-changeable,” i.e. changeableness. ὁρῶντας and λογιζομένους are accusative, agreeing with ἡμᾶς as subject of the infinitive. εὐδία, fair weather at sea, against χειμών, storm: the sailors' pair, drawn from the fishermen's own world.
